tier_reason: First-party README Performance table (TurboRes 1.2.0 vs FFmpeg 7.1.1 CLI and ffmpeg.wasm on an Apple M4 MacBook Air) matches every quoted number, and the harness is public (benchmark/benchmark-turbores.html, benchmark/benchmark-ffmpeg-native.sh, benchmark/benchmark-ffmpeg-wasm.html) with Zig flags in scripts/build-zig.sh. It is not A because the browser/wasm engine and version that JIT-compile the TurboRes side are never named (same rule that kept galois at C and let pare reach A only with a pinned Chromium build), the native FFmpeg build is unstated, and the single-threaded TurboRes and ffmpeg.wasm configurations are not in the committed scripts.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: TurboRes: Zig 0.16, zig build-exe -target wasm32-freestanding -O ReleaseSmall -mcpu=generic+atomics+bulk_memory+multivalue+nontrapping_fptoint+reference_types+sign_ext+simd128 -fno-single-threaded --shared-memory --import-memory (scripts/build-zig.sh --release, called by scripts/build.sh). Browser/wasm engine and version used for the table not stated. Native FFmpeg 7.1.1 build provenance and flags not stated; ffmpeg.wasm row uses @ffmpeg/ffmpeg 0.11.6 with @ffmpeg/core 0.11.0 from unpkg.
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers on one Apple M4 laptop; the browser (and so the wasm JIT) is not named. Baseline weakness: FFmpeg 7.1.1's ProRes IDCT has SIMD only on x86 (libavcodec/proresdsp.c calls ff_proresdsp_init_x86 under ARCH_X86 and nothing for aarch64), so on the M4 native FFmpeg ran its scalar C IDCT while TurboRes uses wasm SIMD128; the 2-3x lead over native FFmpeg may shrink on x86. Harness asymmetry: TurboRes pre-demuxes all packets into memory (Mediabunny) and runs 3 warm-up passes, while the FFmpeg CLI script ((11-loop rtime minus 1-loop rtime)/10 with -f null) includes mov demuxing and file reads; the VideoToolbox row (-hwaccel videotoolbox without a hardware output format) includes copying frames back to system memory. benchmark-turbores.html is the multithreaded variant only and benchmark-ffmpeg-wasm.html hard-codes 10 threads, so the single-threaded rows are not reproducible from committed code; the benchmark hard-codes proresFourCc 'apch' for every file, so the 4444 file is decoded under the 422 HQ profile (10-bit output scale vs FFmpeg's yuva444p12le). Correctness: the README says decoding is bit-exact, but PR #3 (merged 2026-07-09, after the 1.2.0 benchmark update of 2026-07-02) fixed 4444 (ap4h/ap4x) output values that were 4x too small and reported Y/U/V only 84-87% bit-identical to FFmpeg 6.0 (max difference 2) and 97.2-97.7% to VideoToolbox (float AAN IDCT), so outputs are close but not bit-exact; the 'apch' path used by the benchmark was not affected by that bug. Release build uses ReleaseSmall. Test videos are hosted on an external R2 bucket. A second merged record of the same repo exists (paper:turbores-aslang-registry, category assemblyscript-and-wasm-langs).

notes: All README numbers confirmed (single-threaded 42/128/158/450 FPS vs native FFmpeg 15/55/57/161; multithreaded 250/763/920/2310 vs 107/342/375/948, VideoToolbox 160/256/464/466, ffmpeg.wasm 84/288/295/706); metadata confirmed (MPL-2.0, 208 stars, 88 commits, last commit 2026-07-14, not a fork). Shortcomings to record: browser unstated, native FFmpeg on aarch64 lacks SIMD ProRes IDCT, pre-demuxed input vs CLI demux, single-threaded configs not scripted, 'bit-exact' claim contradicted by PR #3 (max diff 2 vs FFmpeg), 4444 scale bug fixed after the benchmark (not on the benchmarked apch path). paper:turbores-aslang-registry is a second record of this repo and probably wants decision duplicate.

tier_reason: dmonad/crdt-benchmarks is a well-known third-party suite, but it never measures Automerge 2.x against the old JS Automerge in one run: the 6.7x and 272x ratios come from the current table (i5-8400, Node 20.5.0, Automerge 2.1.10) and an 'older results' table with no machine or Node version, so this is a cross-run comparison, which goes to D under the PostgreSQL/MySQL/ODB precedent. In the same-run table the wasm Automerge is slower than the pure-JS Yjs (and Loro) on every quoted row, so no valid same-run win over a JS equivalent exists.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Cross-run only (two separate tables of the crdt-benchmarks README, different runs, Yjs 13.3.0 vs 13.6.11): B1.1 append 6000 chars 365 ms (Automerge 2.1.10, wasm) vs 2460 ms (Automerge 0.14.1, JS) = 6.7x (derived from page data); B1.3 prepend 307 ms vs 83,488 ms = 272x (derived from page data); B4 editing trace 14,326 ms vs 489,104 ms = 34x (derived from page data). Normalised to Yjs in each run, Automerge went from 8.1x slower to 1.9x slower on B1.1 and from 298x slower to 2.6x slower on B1.3 (derived from page data). Same run: Automerge 2.1.10 is slower than Yjs on B1.1 (365 vs 188 ms), B1.3 (307 vs 119 ms) and B4 (14,326 vs 5,714 ms), and slower than Loro (120, 81, 3,089 ms).
corrections.caveats: Cross-run comparison: the older table (Automerge 0.14.1, Yjs 13.3.0, delta-crdts 0.10.3) states no machine or Node version, while the current table was run on an Intel Core i5-8400 with Node 20.5.0; the baseline is the project's own predecessor. Within one run Automerge 2.1.10 (Rust compiled to wasm) is slower than pure-JS Yjs and than Loro on the quoted B1.1, B1.3 and B4 rows, so it is not faster than the leading JS equivalent. The suite is maintained by the Yjs author; memUsed excludes wasm memory; the README notes Automerge does B4 in about 1 s when all edits go in a single change() transaction. The benchmarked 2.1.10 is outdated: the repository README now describes Automerge 3 (about 10x lower memory use), which the suite does not measure. The repo's own edit-trace harness (rust/edit-trace) commits no numbers.

notes: Numbers quoted in the record all appear in dmonad/crdt-benchmarks README (365 vs 2460 ms, 307 vs 83,488 ms, 14,326 vs 5,714 ms), but only across two tables from different runs; one WebSearch found the Automerge 2.0 announcement claims large gains without quantifying them in the snippet, and the repo commits no comparison numbers. Metadata confirmed: MIT, 6.7k stars, 273 forks, 1,731 commits, last commit 2026-10-09, not a fork. Shortcomings: cross-run only, slower than Yjs and Loro in the same run, measured version 2.1.10 predates Automerge 3, suite run by a competitor's author.

tier_reason: Independent third-party measurement: ChainSafe/bls (a wrapper by another team) times herumi's wasm build against pure-JS noble-bls12-381 and native blst with public code (benchmark/index.ts, benchmark/noble.ts, benchmark/runner.ts, benchmark/params.ts) and publishes the ops/s table in its README; it falls short of A because the CI runner CPU, Node version and the 2020 wasm build flags are not stated and the CI run page is gone (404).

corrections.claimed_speedup: ChainSafe/bls README (ops/s, herumi wasm vs noble JS vs blst native): verify 47.674 vs 17.906 vs 326.38 (herumi 2.7x noble, derived from page data); verifyAggregate (30) 51.151 vs 18.372 vs 453.29 (2.8x, derived from page data); verifyMultiple (30) 3.5233 vs 2.0286 vs 34.497 (1.7x, derived from page data); aggregate pubkeys (30) 2898.9 vs 1875.0 vs 15686 (1.5x, derived from page data); aggregate sigs (30) 1033.0 vs 526.25 vs 6373.4 (2.0x, derived from page data); sign 108.81 vs 10.246 vs 925.49 (10.6x, derived from page data). Native blst is 5-10x faster than herumi wasm.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the measured 2020 build (then built with Emscripten); since v1.5.0 src/bls_c.js is built with clang (wasm32), wasm-ld and wasm-opt via make -C src, now generated by a GitHub Action.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 31 stars, 15 forks; the WASM fallback backend of ChainSafe/bls (106 stars, Apache-2.0), which uses blst native bindings by default in Node
corrections.caveats: Third-party numbers from a ChainSafe CI run around late 2020 (run 1513710175; the run page now returns 404), so CPU, Node version and library versions are not recoverable; herumi has since reported about 1.1x (2022), 10% and 4% (2024) speedups and switched from Emscripten to clang in v1.5.0, and noble-bls12-381 (^0.7.2 in benchmark/package.json) is deprecated in favour of the much faster @noble/curves, so both sides are stale. Harness asymmetries: noble's verify, verifyAggregate and sign inputs are pre-hashed to G2 in prepareTest (hash-to-curve excluded from noble's timing, included in herumi's), which favours noble; noble ran 10 runs and herumi/blst 100, each a plain mean with no warm-up, which can penalise the JIT-compiled pure-JS noble. Not compared with herumi's own library compiled natively (blst native is a different library). No LICENSE file in the repo: the README says 'modified new BSD License' with a BSD-3-Clause link and package.json declares BSD-3-Clause.

notes: All quoted ops/s numbers match the ChainSafe/bls README table; metadata confirmed (31 stars, 235 commits, last commit 2026-09-17 'bump mcl to v4.10' / v1.7.0, not a fork, BSD-3-Clause per README and package.json but no LICENSE file). Shortcomings to record: stale 2020 CI numbers with unstated CPU/Node, deprecated noble-bls12-381 baseline, 10 vs 100 runs, noble timed without hash-to-curve, CI run page gone. Not a duplicate: herumi/mcl and herumi/bls are not in the verified lists.
